value: A political agitation in a town blocked a road in breach of a prohibitory order. Protesters damaged public buses, and one town bus had its seats set alight. Two buses carrying university students on an educational tour had been parked nearby. The bus carrying 47 female students was then approached by men who carried petrol in plastic cans. One man sprinkled petrol inside the bus through a window shutter while another sprinkled petrol through the second shutter, then a match was lit and thrown into the bus and it caught fire while students were still inside. The teachers on board pleaded with the men to stop. Students escaped through the front entrance, some stretched out through the shutters and were pulled out by male students, but three students could not escape and were burnt to death, and about twenty others received burn injuries. The driver and cleaner of the bus stated that two men on a motorcycle stopped beside the bus; one sprinkled petrol and both fled, the motorcycle engine having been kept running. Injured students and teachers identified the accused in a test identification parade held in jail and in court, with the identification process conducted by a Judicial Magistrate who prepared reports. Several initial investigators conducted the investigation in a charged atmosphere, after which the case was transferred to a specialised investigation unit. One accused was arrested later and gave a confessional statement. Post-mortem examinations were conducted on the three deceased students.

The accused jumped over the front wall, broke the outside bulbs and ran away. Around 12.30 AM the accused returned by scaling the door and caught the daughter-in-law's hand. She raised an alarm and the complainant woke up, after which the accused ran away. The complainant's FIR statement and testimony described the incident this way. Both said the accused lived 15-16 houses away and the families were not on visiting terms. value: The victim, a woman, lived on the first floor of a family house with her adult son; a relative of the accused lived on the ground floor with his wife. The accused, who lived in another city, was a regular visitor to the house. On the day of the incident the accused arrived by car at about 11.30 a.m. The ground-floor occupant's wife offered the accused a meal, and the accused said the accused would eat with the ground-floor occupant. Shortly afterwards the household maid heard screams from the victim's room. At about 2.30 p.m. the victim's son came to collect money and found the room locked from inside. He heard the accused talking on a telephone and asked the accused to open the door, which the accused refused. The ground-floor occupant also asked for the door to be opened, and the accused replied that the door would be opened only when police arrived. When police arrived, the accused opened the door and stated that the accused had killed the victim. The accused was holding a blood-stained sword, and the accused's clothing and hands were blood-stained. The victim was lying on a bed, her body smeared with blood. The sword, its sheath, blood-stained bedsheets and a gold bala were seized, and the accused's clothing and hand washings were taken. The post-mortem examination recorded seventeen injuries, all but three of them incised wounds that could be caused by a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword. The accused gave no explanation for being in the locked room or for holding the blood-stained sword. An injury report on the accused recorded an examination time of 11.30 a.m., which the accused relied on to suggest being in police custody at that time; its author was not examined as a witness.

A married woman aged about 24 was found dead in the bedroom of her matrimonial home about three years after her marriage. Her death was caused by strangulation and burning. The victim's father alleged that after about six months of marriage the accused, her husband and mother-in-law, repeatedly demanded a Maruti car as dowry. He stated that the victim told him of being tortured and maltreated for non-fulfilment of the demand, both over the telephone and on visits to her parental home. About three months before the death, the father and a relative went to the matrimonial home to try to resolve the matter. They were humiliated and told not to return without meeting the demand. The post mortem by a panel of three doctors recorded a ligature mark about 31 by 7 centimetres around the neck, a half-burnt cloth with a knot tied around the neck, superficial to deep burns over the body, and a smell of kerosene. The cause of death was recorded as suffocation with shock from strangulation with simultaneous ante-mortem burns. Investigators recovered blood and a bloodstained bindi from a balcony outside the room, broken bangles inside the room, and a burnt cordless phone and burnt wire stuck with the body. The body was found in a corner of the bedroom. The accused claimed the death was suicide. The mother-in-law lodged a police report stating that the victim had committed suicide. Both accused were absconding for some days before the husband surrendered and then the mother-in-law did.

A further document dated 4 June 1982, written on stamp paper, recorded that the accused was living a normal family life as a married couple with the victim and that the victim was the accused's wife. Voter lists for 1984, 1988 and 1993 for the village where the couple lived showed the victim as the accused's wife. Five witnesses testified that the two lived together as husband and wife at several places of the accused's official posting, including a block in Hazaribagh district, and that a son was born during the cohabitation. The accused was also said to have celebrated the birth of the couple's daughter and son with friends. value: On the night of 6 January 2000, the accused was on security duty as guard commander at a technical battery area of an army unit, armed with a 7.62 mm self-loading rifle and 20 cartridges. Following a report that stones had been thrown at the guard hut, the security junior commissioned officer ordered a Quick Reaction Team to be summoned. The team reached the guard hut at about 10.30 p.m., where the vehicle was challenged by the sentry on duty. Team members got out and moved to the right and left to locate the person who had thrown the stones. The accused ran toward one team member, the victim, while another team member followed and warned that the person being run toward was a member of the Quick Reaction Team and should not be fired upon. Despite this warning, the accused fired three shots from a distance of 8 to 10 feet, killing the victim at the spot. The accused was quickly apprehended by a sentry and the security junior commissioned officer. When questioned about what had been done, the accused replied 'MAINE JO KARNA THA KAR DIYA'. Evidence presented included the testimony of several army personnel who witnessed the shooting, post-mortem observations regarding the firing distance, and empty cartridge cases lifted from the site that matched the issued weapon.

value: The victim had a long-running rivalry with the accused, arising from competition for a liquor shop licence near a railway station and later incidents, including an assault, a theft complaint and an earlier attempt on the victim's life a few months before the shooting. On the day in question, the victim was returning on a cycle from a government food-grain depot with two companions, who were about 15 to 20 paces behind him. The accused arrived on a motorcycle carrying a double-barrelled gun. On seeing the accused, the victim left his cycle and ran toward a neighbouring plot. A single shot was fired, and the victim fell with gunshot injuries. The accused fled, leaving the motorcycle at the scene. The two companions stated that they did not chase the accused. The victim was taken by bullock cart to a hospital, and a complaint was lodged at the police station. A magistrate recorded the victim's statement at the hospital, noting the victim was in a serious condition. A doctor examined the victim and found multiple gunshot wounds on the chest, abdomen, arms, hand and thigh, and a further wound on the neck. The victim died later that night. A post-mortem examination found multiple gunshot wounds of entry, consistent with the medical examination. Investigators collected the motorcycle, a basket of goods, blood-stained and unstained earth, wads from the spot, and blood-stained clothing of the victim.

value: On the afternoon of 25 May 1999, around 12.30 p.m., the victim was at a tyre shop. The prosecution case was that about ten to twelve armed persons, carrying gupties, swords, knives and gandasas, surrounded the victim and attacked him, inflicting multiple incised and penetrating wounds to the head, face, neck, chest, abdomen, back and arms. He said the victim's brother arrived about ten minutes after the removal, and that he had given no names because he had not seen the attack. Three police witnesses, including the constable and driver who lifted the body, stated that the victim's brother and two other alleged eyewitnesses were not present. The post-mortem report recorded excessive haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver as the cause of death. Three named eyewitnesses testified that they saw the attack.

value: On 22 March 1998, the accused reported to a section in-charge that the victim and another soldier had abused him with a derogatory word. The section in-charge questioned them and they denied it. The accused also reported a heated exchange with the victim the previous night. Later that day the victim returned to the barrack after lunch and lay on his cot near the door. Another soldier, who had also just returned to the barrack, saw the accused approach the door wearing a half T-shirt and a lungi. The accused took a knife hidden in the lungi and stabbed the sleeping victim once on the right side of the chest. The eyewitness shouted at the accused and others gathered; the accused was separated from the victim, who was taken to hospital and later died. The regimental medical officer testified that the only external injury was the knife wound. The knife, made of iron with a sharp edge, was among the evidence collected. The victim had also given a dying declaration to another soldier, who testified. The eyewitness could not link the stabbing to the earlier abuse or argument. Timing evidence showed about 40 to 45 minutes between the accused's return from the higher officer's office and the stabbing, during which the accused and the victim were in the same barrack without any conversation.

value: On the night of 11-12 December 2000, the family had gone to bed after dinner around 9 pm. A quarrel broke out between the accused and his wife around midnight, which escalated into an assault around 1 am. The quarrel reportedly arose from the accused's frustration over the sale of family property and his accusations against his wife. During the assault the accused used a sharp-edged cutting weapon on his wife, who was pregnant, causing numerous incised wounds. The accused's mother intervened to save the wife and was also cut with the weapon. The noise and cries woke the couple's young daughter, who was sleeping in an adjacent room and began to cry. The accused went into that room and struck the child, who sustained two injuries, including a fracture, and died. The wife testified as an injured eyewitness to the sequence of events and stated that she did not see the accused strike the child. A post-mortem found the cause of death to be coma resulting from head injuries sustained 24 to 36 hours earlier, consistent with the blunt side of a weapon. Medical reports recorded fifteen injuries on the wife, who was hospitalised for about one and a half months, and six injuries on the mother, two of whose fingers were later amputated. After the incident the accused bolted the doors from inside, refused to open them to police, and threatened to kill anyone who entered. Police, assisted by villagers, forced the door open and found the accused inside the house armed with an Aruval, with the injured women and the child in the house. An observation mahazar recorded writings on the inner walls of the house. Prosecution witnesses, including the mother, gave evidence about the accused's treatment for mental health concerns.

value: The accused was the commanding officer of a military supply depot whose butchery supplied dressed meat, obtained from a private contractor, to indenting army units. The butchery was run by a supervisory officer, a veterinary officer, junior commissioned and non-commissioned officers, and the accused had overall charge of the depot. After complaints about irregularities, a team of three officers from a central investigating agency and two army officers carried out a surprise inspection of the butchery on 14 February 1990. The inspection team checked eleven vehicles returning from the butchery with meat. Of 1411.2 kg of dressed meat issued to various units, 14.5 kg was found to be heart, which was not an acceptable part of the carcass under the contract's special conditions. During discussions with the inspecting officers, the accused remarked that, to the best of the accused's knowledge, heart was an edible offal that could be issued on demand of units. The accused repeated this in a confidential report dated 15 February 1990. The prosecution case was that this remark amounted to accepting heart as part of the dressed meat with intent to defraud the government. There was no evidence that the accused had instructed heart to be accepted or that heart was regularly accepted. The supervisory and veterinary officers were separately charge-sheeted and punished. The prosecution also alleged that reserve stocks of animals were not maintained in the butchery between 11 and 22 March 1990, and that passed animals were not segregated from the contractor's other animals, contrary to the butchery's standard operating procedure.

value: The victim was found dead inside a house in Delhi, having suffered bullet injuries to the left side of the temporal region and the left side of the abdomen. Police received a telephone call about the body on the evening of 23 July 2005. The victim's wife, who had been in Chandigarh, stated that the victim had left Chandigarh for Delhi carrying a licensed revolver, a mobile phone SIM and a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs intended for negotiating a settlement. The sum was not fully recovered. Records showed that the victim's SIM became inactive on the date of the murder and that two incoming calls from a Chandigarh telephone had been received on that day. Investigators then found that a handset bearing a particular IMEI number, which had been used with the victim's SIM, was used with a SIM registered in the name of the accused, immediately after the murder and until 2 August 2005. Service provider records confirmed the registration of that SIM in the accused's name. Police recovered three mobile handsets from the accused, one bearing the IMEI number of the victim's handset, and a revolver with live and spent cartridges that had belonged to the victim. Recovery memos bore the signatures of the accused's brother and father, who later asserted that their signatures had been taken on blank papers. The accused was arrested on 6 August 2005. A deposit of Rs. 9,000 had been made into a bank account in the accused's name two days after the murder.

value: In the early hours of 10 April 2003, a fire broke out in the residential flat where the accused lived with his wife and three children. Witnesses testified that the accused and his wife were heard quarrelling loudly at about midnight on the previous night, and that the accused was seen returning to the flat around that time. The accused's family had a history of tension, and witnesses described the accused as a dictatorial and hot-tempered man who had beaten his wife with a leather belt and whose children resented his behaviour. Household servants sleeping in the veranda heard a loud noise at about 4.00 to 4.30 a.m. and found the flat on fire with a strong smell of petrol. After the fire was extinguished, the bodies of the wife, son and two daughters were found burnt in the children's bedroom. A witness had earlier seen a new ten-litre plastic can containing petrol in the flat. The accused's car was missing and he was not found at the scene. Police later recovered a red bucket from the flat's bathroom on the accused's own disclosure, and a chemical analysis of the bucket showed the presence of petrol. The electrician who inspected the premises found no short circuit. Post-mortem examinations showed that all four victims died from burning. The accused's own account of having left to visit a sick relative was not accepted by the investigators.

He went to the rear of the house and said he saw the victim lying in a room, and when he asked the accused about her, the accused denied she was there. The accused's son later went to the police and reported that the accused had killed the girl and that her body lay under a cot in the house. Police went to the house with the victim's father and recovered the body from under the cot, while the accused was sitting outside. Blood was found on a bed-sheet, on the cot and on the floor beneath it, and the clothing and cloth pieces were found to contain human blood. The post-mortem found injuries consistent with sexual assault, ligature marks on the neck and death by strangulation. value: The victim, the accused's wife, was found unconscious in a chair in the rented first-floor flan the couple shared in a house owned by a landlady, and was taken to hospital by the landlady and her maid. The accused, who worked as a computer faculty member, arrived at the hospital later. The victim was declared dead the following day after repeated cardiac arrests. The post-mortem found cyanosis, froth in the mouth and nostrils, and a yellowish liquid in the stomach that smelled of bitter almonds. Forensic analysis of the stomach and organ samples found cyanide. The prosecution's case was that the accused bought a cold drink bottle from a general store, mixed cyanide into it at the house, and gave it to the victim, who had asked for a cold drink. The shopkeeper testified about the sale, but said he did not remember the buyer well and did not know where the buyer lived. A goldsmith said to have sold cyanide to the accused was examined, but he testified that police had coerced him into making his statement. A statement attributed to the accused before police, witnessed by two panch witnesses, was repudiated; one panch witness did not support it. An empty Limca bottle was later recovered from a shelf in the couple's bedroom and was found to contain cyanide, but the bottle reached the laboratory weeks after its recovery.

value: On an afternoon in April 2000, the victim, a sitting state legislator, was riding as a pillion passenger on a motorcycle driven by an informant on a road near a coal-handling site. The informant heard a gunshot from behind and saw a black motorcycle without a registration number running alongside on the left. It was driven by the accused, with a second man on the pillion holding a pistol. The pillion rider fired at close range; the victim was struck in the head, slumped onto the informant, and both men fell to the road. The driver stopped a short distance ahead. The second man walked back, threatened the informant to leave, fired another shot at the victim, pushed the body down the roadside slope, and both men rode away towards a nearby town. Two bystanders who arrived afterwards stated that they had earlier seen the accused riding the same unregistered motorcycle with a pillion passenger in the area. The informant's motorcycle was seized from the scene. A second black unregistered motorcycle was seized from premises linked to the accused; its registration certificate was in another person's name. Two 9 mm empty cartridges were recovered from the scene. The informant's blood-stained T-shirt and torn jeans were seized. A medical examination that evening recorded injuries consistent with a fall. The post-mortem recorded gunshot wounds to the head as the cause of death. The informant identified the pillion rider in court, and one bystander identified him in a test identification parade. Investigators did not send the clothing to a forensic laboratory or the cartridges to a ballistics expert, and the weapon was never recovered. Evidence of a dispute over a petrol pump and of the victim's action against coal theft was also given.

value: The victim, a married woman, died within the matrimonial home. The prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence. Several witnesses who were relatives of the victim, including the victim's father, a cousin and a brother, deposed that the victim had been subjected to consistent ill-treatment at the matrimonial home. According to their evidence, the accused was having an illicit relationship with a sister-in-law, and when the victim complained about this, the victim was tortured. The victim had written letters to her father complaining of this ill-treatment; one such letter was placed on record as an exhibit. Witnesses also spoke of beating and visible injury marks on the victim. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor, who recorded two incised injuries on the body: a deep incised wound on the front of the neck, at the level of the thyroid cartilage, which had completely cut the trachea and cut major neck veins, and a second incised wound on the upper right side of the abdomen through which the small intestine protruded. The doctor's evidence was that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. The body showed some petrification because of the time gap between death and the post-mortem examination. The victim's identity was confirmed by the father, a cousin and a brother, and the hospital released the body to the father, who had it cremated. The defence case was that the victim had been suffering from jaundice and died a natural death. The only witness called in support was not shown to be a medical practitioner and stated only that the victim had been referred for treatment to Patna on 02.09.1993; no record of jaundice treatment was produced.

value: The victim, a seventeen-year-old woman, went with her younger sister to meet her aunt at the aunt's house. While they were talking, a group of persons including the accused arrived at the house, and the victim was forcibly lifted into a blue Maruti van despite raised alarm by the aunt, her husband and neighbours. The victim was taken to a vacant building near a bridge and placed in a separate room, where two men were said to have sexually assaulted her while others fondled her body; one was said to have inserted a finger into her anus and another bit her cheek. The victim was later taken in the same van to another house, where she was beaten, and she then escaped by bus to meet her mother and sister, to whom she narrated the incident. An FIR was recorded the following night. The FIR described one man as short-statured with a beard and did not name the accused. value: The victim, a woman who had married a man against her family's wishes, lived with her husband and young child in a house owned by another family. About six years after the marriage, the accused, a paternal uncle of the victim, telephoned the victim on 14 August 2002, saying her grandmother was seriously ill and that he would come to pick her up. A household member was sent to a telephone booth to guide him. The accused arrived, was brought to the house, and was introduced by the victim as her uncle. The victim left with the accused on a white scooter, leaving her young son behind. Her husband returned that evening and was told she had gone with the accused. She did not return that night or the next day. The husband lodged a report on 16 August 2002 that she had gone to relatives and had not been seen since. Her body was recovered later that day. A second report then recorded the husband's suspicion, for the first time, that the accused had lured her away and killed her. A post-mortem found death by asphyxia due to smothering, with her scarf pushed into her mouth. The accused was arrested on 7 September 2002, and jewellery the victim was said to have been wearing when she disappeared was recovered from the accused's pockets. The prosecution relied on last-seen testimony from household members and a press reporter who saw the victim and the accused at a bus stand, on the jewellery recovery, and on the post-mortem findings. Witnesses who had seen the accused gave statements to a magistrate about four months later, and one witness identified the accused in court more than two years after the event.

value: The victim was admitted to a hospital with serious burn injuries after a fire at the matrimonial home. A girl aged about five to six years was found dead on a cot in a village where she was staying with her blind, infirm maternal grandmother, who was too poor and unable to care for her. The girl's grandmother's thatched house had collapsed, so the grandmother and the girl used to sleep in a house very close by, which belonged to the accused. The victim's mother was first told the girl had died of paralysis, and the body was buried on a riverbank. Later, the mother received information from several villagers that the girl had been raped and killed by the accused, and she asked for the body to be exhumed. After an order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, the body was dug out and examined on 3.2.1996 by two doctors. They found multiple contusions on the face, neck, shoulder and back, and vaginal injuries including lacerations, and stated that the death was caused by shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem vaginal injuries. One witness deposed that he had been returning home at about 9.00 p.m. with a companion, heard whispering near the accused's house, and focused a torch and saw the accused raping the girl beneath a tree outside the house. The companion raised a cry, villagers gathered, and the accused ran away. Another witness deposed that the accused had confessed the crime to him in the presence of two others. A part of a bed sheet and white cloth were recovered during the investigation, and forensic examination found human blood and semen on them, as well as on a vaginal swab taken by the doctor. The accused was arrested at a road junction in the early hours of the following day while waiting for transport. Several other witnesses did not support the prosecution account.

value: The victim was married in June 2002 in an arranged marriage. At the marriage, a dowry of Rs 25,000 was promised by the victim's side; Rs 15,000 was paid then and the balance of Rs 10,000 was promised within about four months. The victim's father could not pay the balance. The prosecution alleged that the accused, the victim's spouse and mother-in-law, pressed for the balance, harassed the victim for non-payment, refused to send the victim to the parental home, and that the victim had told relatives about the ill-treatment. A witness said that the couple was happy for the first months and that quarrels followed. On one visit to the parental home, the spouse demanded a fan, a ring and Rs 1,000 in cash, along with the balance dowry; when these were not met, the spouse left the victim there. On 15 February 2003, around 11 a.m., the accused left a witness in the house on an errand. When the witness returned, the victim was found hanging from a beam with a saree. The victim's parents came, cut the victim down and took the victim to hospital, where the victim was declared dead. Police registered the report, seized the saree used for hanging, photographed the scene and arranged a post-mortem. The doctor found an oblique ligature mark on the front and left sides of the neck and an abrasion on the chin, all antemortem, and recorded asphyxia from hanging as the cause of death. The victim's father's account was corroborated by two other witnesses. One witness stated that the dowry of Rs 15,000 was handed over at the marriage and that the balance was not paid. The witnesses described the persistent dowry demands and beating and abuse of the victim.

value: The victim, a married woman, died from extensive burn injuries within 35 days of her marriage to the accused. Hospital records noted that, according to the accused, she was burned by a stove while preparing tea and bread in the kitchen. Police recovered from the kitchen a 20-litre cane with about a litre of kerosene, a quilt, pillows, a piece of cloth soaked in kerosene, and the victim's clothes, which smelled of kerosene. The prosecution alleged that shortly after the marriage the accused demanded Rs.40,000 from the victim's father for business purposes. The father refused, and the accused remarked that he knew how to obtain money through his own daughter. The accused later pledged the victim's jewels with a third party for Rs.11,000. The victim was also alleged to be upset about the accused's illicit relationship with his niece, who lived in the same house. Several witnesses, including the victim's father, a neighbour, a cousin and a relative, testified that the victim had complained to them about the money demands, the relationship and her unhappiness in the marriage. The victim was taken to a government hospital and then a medical college hospital, where she died nine days after the incident. The treating civil surgeon recorded a forehead injury with suspicion of fracture and eyelid swelling, consistent with a wall clock blow. A forensic doctor attributed death to the head injuries. value: The accused and the victim's family lived in the same village and owned adjoining agricultural land. A dispute existed over the use of a way to reach their fields. On the morning of the incident, the victim and the complainant attempted to reach their field to sow seeds but were obstructed by one of the accused, who abused and threatened them. Later that day, the complainant was told by a neighbour that several of the accused were waiting on a road to assault the victim. The complainant rode a bicycle to the spot and, from about 200 metres away, saw a group beating the victim with a cycle chain and stones while abusing him. The group then turned on the complainant and assaulted him with a cycle chain and stones until a bystander intervened. The complainant found the victim bleeding heavily from the head and with beating marks over the body. The victim was taken to a rural hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem recorded 19 external and 4 internal injuries, all ante-mortem, with death due to shock from haemorrhage. The doctor stated that some injuries were caused by a cycle chain and others by stones, and that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death. The complainant's 11 injuries were certified by the same doctor and attributed to hard blunt objects and a cycle chain. Police arrested the accused, seized blood-stained clothing, and recovered the cycle chain and stones on the basis of information from the accused. Chemical analysis detected human blood on the clothing of the accused and the victim, although the blood group of the accused's sample was inconclusive. A second eyewitness supported the complainant's account. In oral evidence the complainant named fewer assailants than in his written complaint.

value: The prosecution case is that the victim disliked a man visiting his house and suspected him of having an illicit relationship with the victim's wife. The victim had forbidden the man from coming to the house and threatened to kill him if he returned. About two days before the incident the man came again and the victim repeated the threat. On the day of the incident, around noon, the victim was sitting in front of a roadside eatery near a bus stand. Two witnesses had just finished taking tea there and saw a verbal altercation between the victim and two accused, one of whom was the man's father. During the altercation, one accused threw a stone which struck the victim on the head. The victim fell, and the other accused struck him several times with a sword, injuring his neck, head and face. People nearby ran away. Witnesses said the attackers fled believing the victim dead. Witnesses tried to help the victim, who was bleeding heavily, and took him to a police station and then toward a hospital, where he died en route. Police witnesses prepared a site plan and seized items from the spot, including the sword and the stone. The post-mortem found several ante-mortem external injuries, including a frontal bone fracture, a crush injury to the cheek, and a neck wound with a vertebral fracture. The doctor opined the injuries were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. The doctor stated that the crush injury could be caused by the stone and the other injuries by the sword. A forensic report found human blood on the blade of the sword and on the stone.

value: The victim was married to the accused in February 1990. The accused was serving in the army and stayed at the matrimonial home only while on leave. The prosecution case was that, soon after the marriage, the accused demanded a motorcycle as dowry and threatened that the victim would not be allowed to remain in the matrimonial home if the demand was not met. Relatives of the victim, including her brother and a village companion, intervened and pacified the accused on more than one occasion. In the days before the victim's death in September 1993, the demand was renewed, the accused harassed the victim and beat her. On 16 September 1993 the accused's brother visited the victim's brother's village and reported that the victim had died after suffering an electric shock. When the victim's brother and others reached the matrimonial village, they learned that the body had already been cremated. Enquiries led the victim's brother to conclude that the victim had been killed for dowry by the accused and the accused's mother. A first information report was lodged on 19 September 1993 and the accused was arrested the same day. The evidence consisted of oral testimony from the victim's brother, a village companion, the victim's father and another witness about the dowry demand and the cruelty, and evidence from the village Sarpanch about the cremation. No doctor who allegedly attended the victim was examined and no medical evidence on the cause of death was produced. The electrocution explanation rested on the accused's brother, who did not testify, and the accused did not mention electrocution in his statement under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

value: On 18 February 2005 at about 6:30 p.m. the victim went to fields near her village to ease herself and did not return. Her family searched but could not find her. During the search the accused was found in the fields. When the victim's mother asked him where her daughter was, he did not respond and ran away from the place. He could not be traced in the village until 21 February 2005, when he was reportedly produced and arrested. The victim's body was found the next morning in daylight in fields belonging to another person, with her neck wrapped in a blue shawl that belonged to her. The family had earlier had a dispute with the accused: some years before, he and a cousin had teased the victim's elder sister on a path, the matter was taken to a village panchayat, and both apologised; the accused was said to have later threatened revenge. Medical examination showed death by asphyxia due to strangulation, ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death. There were multiple abrasions and contusions on the face, chin and back. Forensic examination found blood on the shawl, salwar and underwear of the victim. Human semen was detected on a vaginal swab from the victim. The accused's underwear, taken on his examination after arrest, also showed human semen. The medical evidence indicated the victim had been subjected to sexual intercourse before her death.

value: The victim went out to graze cows and did not return by dusk; the next morning his body was found with injuries in a jungle. The police registered a case, held an inquest, and during investigation a labourer who worked under the victim was apprehended and made a statement implicating two men. The principal evidence is the account of an eyewitness who was grazing cows with the victim in a rubber garden around 2 p.m. At about 4 p.m. the two accused arrived armed with an axe, a lathi and a gun. The first accused struck the victim with the axe; the second struck him with a stick; and the first then took a gun from the jungle and shot him. The eyewitness fled, stating he was afraid because the accused had threatened him with dire consequences if he disclosed the incident. He later told another villager, and subsequently gave a statement to police. A witness stated that around 1.30 p.m. he had seen the victim and the accused grazing cows nearby. The investigating officer's inquest report recorded injuries caused by an axe and a gun. He also recovered the handle of an axe near the body and seized it under a seizure list prepared in the presence of witnesses. Blood-stained wooden sticks and a takkal dao were also found near the body. A charge-sheet was filed against the two accused.

value: According to the prosecution, on the afternoon of 29 March 2000 the victim, a 22-year-old woman, went to a field near an embankment to attend her goats. When she did not return home, her father searched for her along the embankment. While returning, he heard loud laughter from a farm house belonging to the accused. Later he went back to the embankment, shouted for her, and the accused came out of the farm house and looked at him. The father then went down a path and found the victim lying dead on the left side, with a cut injury on her chin and blood oozing from her body. He raised an alarm, and her brother and other villagers gathered. The accused also came to the spot and enquired. The body was taken home, and a Sub-Inspector of Police seized the victim's clothing and prepared a seizure list. The inquest was held and the body was sent for post-mortem. The brother lodged a written complaint at the police out-post, and a case was registered. During investigation, the victim's underwear stained with semen was seized the same day. The accused and an eyewitness labourer were apprehended and interrogated. On the next day, police seized a blue underwear of the accused suspected to have semen stains, a bed sheet, a sporting item and a dao from the farm house. Both underwear items were sent for forensic examination. The post-mortem doctor found death by asphyxia due to throttling, a fractured trachea, bruises on the neck and a cut injury on the chin, and found no spermatozoa in the vaginal smear and no sign of injury on the genital organs. The eyewitness stated that he saw the accused and a companion follow the victim, saw them commit rape and then throttle her, and saw them drag the body into bushes. He said he stayed silent out of fear because both men carried khukris. The victim's father, two brothers and co-villagers gave corroborative evidence about the body and the scene.

value: On the evening of 28 June 2001, a group of about 25 to 30 persons from the village gathered outside the house where the victims were staying. They were armed with swords, gandasis, sabals and sticks. The group surrounded the house, climbed onto its roof and pelted stones, damaging the roof sheets and tiles. Several of the occupants escaped over a common wall into another room. Around midnight, the informant, his wife, his mother and another woman were made to sit on a neighbouring thatched roof. Shortly afterwards, a further group arrived in a jeep, broke open the door of the informant's house and inflicted blows with swords, gandasis and sticks. Three persons died inside the house. Two others were dragged outside and assaulted on the head, face, hands and feet with gandasis and swords, and both died. The attackers burnt two motorcycles belonging to the victims before leaving. The FIR was lodged at 6.45 a.m. on 29 June 2001. The informant explained that the family was too traumatised during the night to go to the police station. Investigators prepared a site plan, conducted autopsies, seized blood-stained clothing and recorded witness statements. Weapons were recovered on information given by accused persons in custody. The eyewitnesses were the informant and close relatives of the deceased. The defence contended that no independent witness was examined. The motive alleged was suspicion that the victims had killed the son of the village leader, which led to revenge.

value: The victim, a 19-year-old student, had known the accused for some time, and the accused had been meeting her outside her school in an attempt to develop intimate relations. On the day in question the accused induced the victim to travel with him to Kurukshetra so that they could get married, and she agreed. At the bus stand, the victim's father and police officers were present, and the accused was apprehended. The victim's father had lodged a complaint alleging enticement and wrongful confinement. The victim was medically examined, and the medical officer deposed that she had indulged in sexual intercourse and was habitual to it. Her statement was recorded before a Magistrate under Section 164 Cr.P.C. The warden, declared hostile, deposed that the victim had stayed in the hostel without permission. value: The victim, a young woman, was a neighbour of the accused in the same village. The victim had lost her mother in early childhood and lived with her brother's family, and her father also lived in the house. The accused used to tease the victim and repeatedly asked her to marry him. On one occasion the victim was alone at home while other family members were at a temple. The accused entered the house and asked for sexual intercourse. The victim refused and said intercourse could only take place after marriage. The accused gagged the victim's mouth with the accused's right hand and had sexual intercourse with the victim. Afterwards the accused told the victim not to reveal the incident to anyone, promising marriage while placing a hand on the victim's head. Over about six months the two were intimate repeatedly at different places, and the accused repeatedly said marriage would follow. During a visit to a temple, the accused refused to marry the victim. The victim told the victim's brother and father, who sought the help of village elders. The elders convened a panchayat and summoned the accused, who again refused to marry. The victim then lodged a complaint with the police on 10 October 2003. Prosecution evidence included the testimony of the victim, the victim's brother and father, four village elders who attended the panchayat, two friends of the accused who had met the victim and the accused at the temple, and a doctor who medically examined the victim.

value: The prosecution case is that the accused approached the victim, a married woman, in an agricultural field at about 6.30 p.m. on 21 December 1987 when she had gone there to relieve herself. The victim alleged that the accused caught hold of her, pushed her to the ground, covered her mouth with one hand, restrained her hands with the other, lifted her petticoat and committed rape on her. She returned home and told her mother-in-law about the incident the same evening. The next day, when her husband returned home, she lodged a complaint at the police station, which was registered as an FIR on 22 December 1987. A doctor who examined her the same evening stated that, as the victim was a married woman habitual to intercourse, no definite opinion could be given on whether she had been subjected to sexual intercourse. No injury was found on her person; the victim explained that she had fallen on her back in a field with a smooth surface where wheat and mustard crops grew. The petticoat and vaginal smear slides were preserved and sent for forensic examination. Police visited the scene on 23 December 1987, seized a blouse, a dhoti and broken bangles, and prepared a site map. The forensic laboratory report recorded spots of semen and spermatozoa on the petticoat. The accused denied having had sexual intercourse with the victim and suggested he had been falsely implicated because of a quarrel with her husband. The victim's mother-in-law denied that suggestion. The victim was not questioned in cross-examination about the seizure of the articles from the field.

At his instruction, police and witnesses went to the spot in a jeep, where the body was recovered from under stones and branches. At the accused's instruction a blood-stained shirt was recovered from under a stone on a road, and it bore blood of the same group as the victim. value: In the early hours of the morning on 8 July 2008, while members of a household were asleep in two rooms of a family dwelling, the accused allegedly attacked family members with the separated parts of a pair of sharp scissors. The accused's spouse and two sons were stabbed multiple times and died at the scene. The accused also stabbed the victim, the accused's daughter, multiple times. When the victim asked why she was being hurt, she was told that the whole family had to go and the accused would follow. The accused then gave her water, held her on his lap, and pressed a pillow over her mouth, but she did not die. The accused left her in that condition, bolted the outer door from outside, and went to a police station to report the incident. A neighbouring relative heard the victim calling for help, opened the door and found the deceased lying in pools of blood. The victim was taken to hospital and treated. The post-mortem examination recorded death from haemorrhagic shock with haemothorax due to multiple stab injuries, and the doctor opined that the injuries could have been caused by the scissors. Blood on the accused's clothing matched the blood group of the accused's deceased spouse. The scissors and clothing were recovered on the accused's disclosure, and blood-soaked material was collected from the spot. The accused's statement to the police, recorded at the station, described the killings and gave a reason for them. The investigation included an inquest, a spot panchnama and photographs.

The post-mortem found 97% ante-mortem burns and death due to shock, with no signs of pregnancy. value: The accused married the victim in 1988 and they lived in a matrimonial house together with the accused's parents and brother. It is alleged that the accused and other household members ill-treated and tortured the victim. During the marriage the victim had a premature delivery. After a later pregnancy in 1993, it is alleged that the accused gave the victim tablets that caused a miscarriage. A child born to the couple did not survive long. On 23 February 1996 the victim poured kerosene over herself and drank some, which was later cleared away. A mediation meeting had been scheduled for that day, and the victim's relatives and a neighbour were to attend. The victim then died by hanging before the meeting took place. A neighbour gave the first information to the police. The case was first registered as an unnatural death and later altered to offences of cruelty and abetment of suicide. The investigating officer seized documents and material objects, examined witnesses, and laid a charge sheet. A post-mortem examination was conducted. The evidence included oral testimony from fifteen witnesses, documentary exhibits, material objects, and evidence that the accused worked abroad and visited India on leave only four times between 1988 and 1996, the last visit being in January-February 1996. The accused had also made efforts toward mediation to settle the differences.

value: On the early morning of the occurrence, two visitors who had arranged by telephone the previous evening to be taken to a plot for earthwork came to the victim's house. They were let in, and tea was prepared for them at the victim's direction. The visitors asked the victim to accompany them on his scooter. As he started the scooter, both visitors drew pistols from the folds of their garments and fired at him. He fell onto the scooter. The victim's mother and wife were in the house and witnessed the shooting. The assailants ran away, and the mother heard a vehicle starting on the other side of the road. The mother gave a statement to police, which led to registration of the first information report. The investigating officer called a fingerprint expert to the house. The expert found two glass tumblers on the table, smeared with tea. He lifted fingerprints from them, sealed them in a packet, and sent them to the fingerprint bureau. There, the seal was found intact, and the prints were compared with specimen prints of two suspects taken in the presence of a Judicial Magistrate. The comparison found the questioned prints similar to the specimen prints. The autopsy showed a lacerated wound on the left side of the chest. It had blackening around it and perforated the left lung, the upper part of the heart and the right lung. The doctor opined that death resulted from shock and haemorrhage due to a firearm injury. Police recovered two pistols with live cartridges, two empty twelve-bore cartridges, the scooter and a footwear from the spot.

value: The victim, a 28-year-old married woman, was admitted to hospital with extensive burn injuries on the night of 9 December 2003, after kerosene oil was poured on her at her matrimonial home and set alight. Burns covered roughly half her body. Once a doctor certified her fit to give a statement, a Magistrate recorded her statement. She said that at about 9.30 to 10.00 p.m. the accused, a husband, a brother-in-law and the brother-in-law's wife, had poured kerosene oil on her and set her ablaze, and that nobody tried to extinguish the fire. She said the husband had an illicit relationship with the brother-in-law's wife, that she quarrelled with him over it, and that after drinking liquor he beat her with a stick and shoes. Investigators inspected the scene, seized burnt clothing, ash and a kerosene lamp, and obtained post-mortem and forensic reports. The post-mortem doctor attributed death to ante-mortem burns sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. A medical examiner noted superficial deep burns across the body and said burns from kerosene falling on the head could not be ruled out. The victim's father testified to dowry harassment, earlier divorce proceedings, panchayat settlements and a telephone call a week before the incident seeking to return to her parents' home. The victim's brother supported this account. No eyewitness saw the incident. The defence case was that the burns were accidental, caused by a lamp falling on the victim in the kitchen, and it relied on the testimony of the victim's eight-year-old daughter. Investigators found the brother-in-law and his wife living separately and recorded no specific act by either of them.

On the following morning, the victim and this witness were summoned to a courtyard on the pretext of a meeting. On arrival, they were tied to a bamboo pole and a tree. Several accused, armed with lathis and tangies (sharp cutting weapons), allegedly beat the victim with lathis while the witness escaped. The victim was beaten to death. The victim's two wives, who had followed him to the courtyard, witnessed the assault. The post-mortem doctor recorded fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, including two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp, stated that all injuries contributed to death, and said a blunt object such as a lathi could cause them. value: On 5 November 1990 a man unknown to the victim was looking for her house in a city and asked a passer-by for directions. The passer-by took him to a second woman, who escorted him to the victim's house. At about 1 p.m. a witness saw him at the victim's door. He said a relative was expected to come to the house; the victim replied that the relative had not arrived. That witness left before the man entered the house. That evening the victim did not come to a neighbour's house to watch television. The neighbour sent a child to call her, and the victim said relatives from her village had arrived and she had to cook for them. Another witness saw her alive at about 8.30 p.m. in the company of more than one person. The next day the victim was found dead in her house, with her belongings scattered. At the scene, an expert found chance fingerprints on a plastic cover bearing a bank's name. Later, an expert reported that the accused's fingerprint matched one of them, using a print taken from the accused on a later date. The accused's blood-stained clothes were seized when he was arrested six days after the killing. A blood sample from him could not be tested for blood group. Ornaments were recovered from several people after the accused led police to them, but none was identified as the victim's. A blood-stained steel rod, hidden under a stone slab, was recovered at the accused's instance. No identification parade was held. The relative the accused had mentioned was not questioned by investigators.

value: On 20 August 2006, at about 2 p.m., the victim, a 17-year-old girl who had taken goats to graze in a forest about half a kilometre from her village, was sitting alone on a footpath when the accused caught hold of her from behind. When she asked why, the accused did not respond. The accused physically abused her body, removed her clothes, made her lie on the ground and committed sexual assault by rape. She raised an alarm but no one came. After leaving, the accused threatened her with consequences if she disclosed the incident. Out of fear she did not tell her parents for several days, but remained tense and distressed. On 2 September 2006 she consumed poison, became unconscious and was taken to several hospitals, finally to a postgraduate institute, where she remained until 10 September 2006. On regaining consciousness she told her father and brother that the accused had raped her on 20 August. A first information report was registered on 11 September 2006, after which she was medically examined. The examining doctor recorded no fresh evidence of bleeding, tear or scratch over the vulva, only a slightly reddened area on the outer mucosa, and noted that the hymen was intact. The doctor also noted that the examination was carried out 21 days after the occurrence. The victim's age was established through a birth certificate, a matriculation certificate and medical age tests. The accused was arrested on 12 September 2006 and a charge sheet was filed. The victim's account was supported by her father and brother.

value: The victim was reported missing around 21 June 1995, and his body was later found floating in a canal, after a chappal was recovered on a path leading to the canal near a bridge. The victim's brother, who had gone searching on a motorcycle, reported seeing a chappal, a saw, two pieces of blade, blood and pieces of meat on the path and the body on the water's surface. A missing-person report was made by the victim's mother, and a first information report was later registered. The prosecution case was that the accused and a co-accused killed the victim on the intervening night of 21/22 June 1995 at the instigation of the victim's wife, with whom the co-accused was alleged to have an illicit relationship, and that the body was thrown into the canal. The accused was alleged to have a grudge over the victim's marriage to the wife and a previous fight with the victim. A family member testified that the victim had been seen with the accused and the co-accused on 21 June 1995. A doctor testified that the victim had been murdered about one week before the post-mortem, which found grievous injuries to the neck and scalp and multiple skull fractures. Recoveries were made on the disclosure statements of the accused and the co-accused: the victim's chappal, and blood-stained shirt and trousers of the accused found in a polythene bag under a bridge. Further blood-stained clothing was recovered hidden near the village. The laboratory reported human blood on the clothes, and blood was also found on a hexa blade and the frame of a saw.

value: Some twenty years after an earlier family dispute, which had caused enmity between two families, a group of seventeen persons, including the two accused, allegedly assembled with the common object of killing the victim. On the night of 30 July 1999, the victim was sleeping on a cot outside his house. The assailants allegedly encircled him and inflicted indiscriminate cuts over his body with an aruval, causing instant death. The victim's two sons intervened to save him and were also injured. After the attack the assailants ran away. The matter was first reported to a police station whose jurisdiction did not cover the place of occurrence. An inspector went to the scene that night and recorded the statement of the victim's wife, and a first information report was registered the next morning. The post-mortem examination recorded fifteen incised wounds, mainly on the neck, chest, shoulder, arm and hand. The victim's two sons were also treated for cut injuries. The victim's wife testified that she had known both accused for a long time because they were closely related, and that she recognised them even though it was dark, relying on a street light and electricity supply at the scene. One injured son initially did not support the prosecution but, when examined, named the two accused as taking part in the attack. A wireman from the electricity board gave evidence that power was supplied at the scene at the relevant time. Recoveries were made on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements.

It was alleged that the accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. A person who accompanied the victim's brother to the hospital testified that the victim had said in their presence that her husband had set her on fire. Neighbours heard a commotion and saw the victim near the gateway, as did a son of the accused from an earlier marriage. A maid servant present at the time could not be examined. value: The victim was married to the accused on 20 June 1995. On 1 March 1996, about nine months after the marriage, she suffered burn injuries. Her statement, recorded by a Chief Judicial Magistrate on 2 March 1996 after a medical fitness endorsement, had two parts. The first part described an accident in which a kerosene stove burst while she was preparing tea. The second part alleged that the accused had been pressing her to bring Rs. One lakh from her parents and had threatened to kill her. It further alleged that the accused had tried to hang her, had earlier tried to burn her at night, and at about 5.30 a.m. had doused her from behind with kerosene and set her alight. She stated that the first part had been tutored by the accused. A First Information Report was registered on the basis of that statement. The victim died on 12 March 1996. The post-mortem examination found superficial to deep burns over most of the body, excluding the face, scalp, both legs, feet and part of the left upper arm. The doctor recorded that the cause of death was ante mortem burns. He agreed that kerosene poured from behind would leave burns on the back, and that a stove burst would ordinarily have affected the face and scalp, which were not burnt. The victim's mother testified that the victim had told her of quarrels over a demand of Rs. One lakh for a piggery farm. The victim's father testified to the same demand and to physical abuse. A letter from the victim to her father demanding Rs. 5,000 was also in evidence. The accused was reported to have donated blood, but the victim died despite it. The case was then converted to a dowry-related offence and a charge sheet was filed.

Houses in the area were damaged and some set on fire, and documents, gold ornaments and cash were taken or burnt. Family members took the victim to hospital, where he was found dead. The post-mortem recorded multiple chop and incised wounds, skull fractures and sub-dural haematoma, with the cause of death given as hemorrhage and shock due to multiple chop wounds with head injury. After disclosure statements by several accused, blood-stained weapons were recovered the day after the incident. value: On the night of 27 June 1997, around 10:00 p.m., the victim, who was a village sarpanch, was sitting and talking with two other persons near a hotel in the village, with street lights on and a chimney burning nearby. Several men arrived at the spot. One carried a sword, another a farsa, another an axe, and the rest lathis. The man with the sword, while abusing the victim and saying he could not escape that day, struck the victim on the head, causing bleeding. Another assailant then struck the victim's head with the farsa, and a third struck the head with an axe, after which the victim fell. Others struck with lathis. Witnesses pleaded for the victim to be spared, and the assailants left after warning the victim not to contest against them in future. The injured eyewitness went to the police station about one kilometre away, and a first information report was registered at 10:45 p.m. The investigating officer visited the scene at 11:10 p.m. and prepared the crime details form. The injured eyewitness was sent for medical examination, completed by 1:30 a.m. The post mortem recorded eight injuries on the body, four of them grievous. The body was taken to the hospital by 7:30 a.m. the next day. Witnesses who came on hearing shouts corroborated the account. The accused were arrested on 28 June 1997, weapons were seized on 29 June 1997 at their instance, and disclosure statements were recorded. The express report was received by the magistrate only on 30 June 1997.

value: On the night of 11 January 2000, the victim was last known to be travelling from a town toward his village after an outing. Around 10 p.m., the victim's brother saw the accused near a tubewell and a bus stand, running away with blood-stained clothes; the brother identified the accused in vehicle headlights and did not then know of any killing. The next morning the victim's wife reported that he had not returned home. The family searched and found the victim's body near a water-supply tubewell, lying in a pool of blood, with wounds on the forehead, nose and eyebrows; his shirt, sweater and slippers lay some distance away. Police recorded the body's location, took possession of the body, a blood-stained brick and clothing, and prepared an inquest. A post-mortem recorded multiple injuries, including contusions on the back, a large chest swelling with fractured ribs and blood in the chest cavity, and lacerated wounds on the forehead and above the right eye; the examining doctors stated that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. In the early hours of the next day the accused attended a government hospital, where a doctor recorded a superficial incised wound on the back of the left forearm with a corresponding cut in the shirt. Later, a witness stated that the accused had told him that on the earlier night he had quarrelled with the victim after both drank liquor and had struck him with a brick. On disclosure by the accused, police recovered blood-stained clothes concealed in a wooden box in the accused's house. Forensic analysis found the same blood group ('O') on the recovered clothes and on the victim's clothing.

value: The victim, a married woman living in a joint household with her husband and his parents and relatives at Morbi, was found hanging from a ceiling fan at the marital home on 23 March 2000. A family member of the accused telephoned the victim's father, who worked at a bank in Rajkot, to come to the house. The police were informed, and an assistant sub-inspector visited the scene, recorded a statement from the accused's family member, and initially registered the death as accidental. The investigation was then taken over by an inspector. The victim's father arrived later that day and suspected foul play, noting that the accused had repeatedly demanded dowry and that none of them were present at the house when the death occurred. A complaint was lodged and an FIR registered for offences relating to cruelty, dowry death and abetment of suicide. The body was cut down and sent for post-mortem examination. Several witnesses were examined. The victim's father, elder sister and grandfather testified that the victim frequently complained of mental torture and harassment by the accused for bringing insufficient dowry. A close friend of the victim testified that the victim had told her of such harassment. Photographs of the body and the inquest panchnama were placed on record. The accused had absconded for some weeks before surrendering at the police station.

value: On the evening of 1 April 1983, the victim was struck with a stone at about 8.30 pm in a village. About four days earlier, during a festival, the victim had visited the accused's home. Later that night the accused came to the victim's household to assault the victim, alleging that the victim's family had been involved in an incident of knocking at the door of a woman in the accused's household at night with evil intention. Family members intervened, preventing the accused from dragging the victim out, and the accused left with a threat. The victim did not return home that night. The next morning a witness said he had seen the victim with the accused at about 7.30 pm, and two eyewitnesses said they saw the accused beating the victim with a stone at about 8.30 pm. Another witness said he had seen the two together just before the incident. The victim's body was later found near a riverbank. The post-mortem recorded that the face and head were flattened, with multiple irregular lacerated wounds, a disfigured face, pulverized skull and mandible bones, and brain matter flowing from the wounds. The death was attributed to shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem injuries which could have been caused by a stone between 8 and 9 pm. The accused was examined and had three injuries to the face, which the doctor said were caused by a hard blunt object or friction about a day earlier. value: The proprietor of a multi-storied hotel and adjoining club in Indore obtained a building permission in 1993, valid for one year, with renewal required before a set date. A revised building plan was later submitted to the Building Officer, who approved it along with a renewal of the permission, and a completion certificate for the adjoining club was granted shortly afterwards. The prosecution alleged that the revised plan was a complete departure from the original plan, with the built-up area of the hotel increased substantially and that of the club's ground floor decreased markedly. It was alleged that the revision was sanctioned without approval from the high-rise building committee and without electricity, water supply, sewage and fire-safety clearances. It was further alleged that the completion certificate was issued only seven days after the revision of the permission, although the club could not plausibly have been completed with all compliances within that time. A Sub-Engineer in the building permission branch was alleged to have made notings in the note sheet favouring the proprietor. value: The victim had been married to the accused only a short time before the incident, and the couple lived in a rented house near the victim's parental home. Both earned a living through daily wage work. On the morning of the incident, the victim went out to answer a call of nature and, on returning somewhat late, was questioned by the accused, who suspected her of infidelity. Despite her attempts to explain, the accused began assaulting her with fists and kicks. He then poured kerosene from a nearby lamp over her and set her ablaze. Her saree caught fire and she ran towards the accused, whose hands were burnt. When she screamed for help, the accused poured water on her. Neighbours and her parents gathered and she was taken to hospital. On the way, she told her mother, sister-in-law and a neighbour what had happened. The neighbour testified only that she said the accused had beaten and kicked her, and did not support the account of kerosene. A sub-inspector recorded her statement at the hospital, on which a First Information Report was registered. After a doctor certified her mental fitness, an executive magistrate recorded a dying declaration naming the accused as the person who poured kerosene and set her on fire. She succumbed to burn injuries on 12 September 2005. The post-mortem found death due to shock and septicaemia caused by 60% burn injuries. A panch witness spoke to a kerosene lamp prepared in an empty liquor bottle in the house. The accused's defence was that the fire was accidental and that he had tried to extinguish it.

value: On a morning in September 1996, near a cycle stand inside a college campus, a group of seven accused, some armed with lathis, knives and khukris, approached two students standing there. They asked the victim and a second student to withdraw their names from a college election. When both refused, the accused assaulted them with their weapons. The victim was struck on the back, neck and face, then ran from the spot, became entangled in wire fencing near a nearby building, and fell. Several accused chased him there and attacked him again with sticks. The second student suffered a head injury. About three hundred students gathered. The victim was taken to hospital and died the next day. The second student lodged a written complaint at a police station, and the shirt he wore was seized. A medical officer examined both injured persons. The victim's frontal bone was found fractured and a lung ruptured; the second student's injuries were consistent with sticks. Eyewitnesses named all the accused and described their individual roles. One witness who had been present gave differing accounts to police and in court. The weapons were not recovered, and a blood-stained shirt was recovered six days after the incident.

value: The victim was riding home from work on a bicycle at about 8:00 p.m. on the evening of the incident, with his younger brother following about 10 to 15 feet behind. Unit officers went to the station, and the accused confessed to stabbing the victim. The forensic surgeon who conducted the autopsy found two ante mortem injuries, one a deep stab wound to the chest that could have caused death. The knife was not recovered. A statement the accused gave during a summary of evidence under the army rules, describing a scuffle and saying he stabbed the victim to free his neck, was proved through the officer who recorded it, with a supporting witness. value: The victim lived in a joint family with a spouse and in-laws after marriage and had a young daughter. Within about two years of marriage, the victim was allegedly tortured by the spouse and in-laws over demands for dowry and for work performance, and was driven out of the matrimonial home. The victim repeatedly left and stayed at shelters and other places, and was returned to the matrimonial home after mediation by relatives. The victim reported demands for Rs.20,000 and filed a maintenance claim, which went unpaid, and lodged a criminal complaint alleging cruelty and dowry harassment. Several witnesses, including the victim's paternal uncle, that uncle's wife, the victim's brother, a social worker and neighbours, testified that the victim was regularly taunted and physically harassed, that the victim was seen sleeping at odd places, and that heated quarrels took place. One witness said the victim came to him for help, claiming the in-laws were trying to kill her, and had burn marks on her hands. On the day of the incident, the victim ran out of the house calling for help, and one in-law described the condition as epileptic fits. The victim was later found to have consumed poisonous tablets. The accused were in the house at the time and took the victim to hospital when the condition became critical. In a dying declaration, the victim stated the tablets were taken by mistake, and the examining doctor recorded that the victim was stable and conscious enough to give a statement. The victim died. A relative lodged a complaint with the police, after which the scene was examined in a panchanama, witness statements were recorded and the accused were arrested.

value: The victim, who is blind and illiterate, lived in her family home with her brothers after her mother left. The accused, a friend of one of the victim's brothers, began visiting the house and talking with the victim. The prosecution case is that about a year before the incident the accused came to the house when the victim was alone, said he loved her and would marry her, and wanted intercourse. The victim tried to avoid it because she was blind, but she submitted after being assured of marriage and support. The accused then came to the house whenever the victim was alone and had intercourse with her. When the victim became pregnant and asked him to marry her, he stopped visiting. The incident was disclosed to the victim's father, who called a village Panchayat. There the accused admitted having had intercourse with the victim but refused to marry her and left. The prosecution's case is that, though blind, the victim could recognise the accused by voice and touch. The matter was investigated, the victim was medically examined, and a charge-sheet was filed. Prosecution witnesses included the victim, a doctor who gave the medical examination report, a radiologist whose X-ray examination estimated the victim's age at approximately 18 years, and persons who attended the Panchayat. The victim testified that she recognised the accused by his voice, that he committed intercourse with her on the pretext of marriage, and that he stopped visiting after she became pregnant. He smothered the flames with a quilt and took the victim on a push-cart to the Rural Hospital, where no doctor was available. A waterman and a maid-servant cleaned the wounds and administered intravenous saline. A police sub-inspector arrived at once and recorded an oral statement from the victim, which bore the victim's thumb impression. In it the victim said the accused, with whom the victim had a love affair and who the victim said had made the victim pregnant, had been asked to marry the victim that evening. On the police requisition, an Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration at the hospital in the presence of two hospital employees, and the victim put a thumb impression on it. The victim was then moved to a district hospital. On 5 March 1989 another Executive Magistrate recorded a different statement, attributing the burns to a falling chimney lamp while the victim slept. That statement had no thumb impression. The victim died on 9 March 1989. A medical officer conducted the autopsy and recorded about 72 per cent burns. The defence case was that the burns were accidental.

The victim's father testified that the accused had visited him on an earlier day, asked that the victim not be sent abroad, and asked that she come to his office; the companion's account was consistent with this. value: The accused and the victim had been married for several years and had two sons. The accused had earlier left police service and worked abroad for a period, sending money home. On the evening of the incident, the accused and the victim returned from a short spiritual retreat. The victim was sent home with the accused's son while the accused went looking for labourers. Later that evening, the accused's brother suffered an epileptic attack at a tea shop, and the accused asked two men to fetch the brother's medical papers from the house. They found the front door open, a lamp lit, and no response from the victim. On entering, they found the victim hanging from a hook in the work area by a saree, with movements, and they raised an alarm. Others arrived, and the saree was cut with a knife and the body brought down. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. The prosecution alleged that the accused smothered and strangled the victim with a plastic rope and then hanged her. A nylon rope and broken glass bangles were recovered from under a cot in the dining room, away from the hanging site. The chemical report found no blood on the rope, and the hairs on it could not be attributed to a sex. The post-mortem doctor recorded pressure abrasion on the neck, a fracture of the hyoid bone, and forehead and facial injuries, but could not say whether death was from suicidal or homicidal hanging. The accused's account was that two unknown persons pushed the accused down on the way home that evening. Three witnesses gave statements at the inquest, and were re-examined nearly four years later, shortly before the charge-sheet was submitted.

value: Two adjacent households, whose members were brothers, had a long-running dispute over land. On the day in question, the son of one household was working in the fields when the accused hurled abuses at him. The son returned home upset and complained to his father. The father went to the rooftop of his house and called the accused over. The accused came with his own son. When the father asked why the accused had abused his son, the accused replied angrily that he was justified and would continue. The accused then ran downstairs, fetched a double-barrelled 12-bore gun and fired at the father, striking him on the side of the head. It was alleged that the accused's son urged the firing. Hearing the commotion, the father's wife and two friends of the son rushed to the rooftop. The accused fired at them. One friend was struck in the abdomen and died, the father's wife was struck in the abdomen, and the other friend was struck in the mouth and head. The injured were taken to hospital, where the friend who was struck died. The accused and his son then fled. In the investigation, the 12-bore gun loaded with two live cartridges was recovered from the accused, and four cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. The site plan prepared by the investigating officer matched the eyewitnesses' account of the place of occurrence. The eyewitnesses included the father and the injured. The medical evidence showed injuries on the deceased and the injured compatible with the weapon used.
