value: The victim, who was involved in real estate, was contacted by phone by a caller offering a land deal, and over several weeks the callers built his confidence in the proposal. On the morning of the planned meeting, the victim went to the site in his own car. Several men arrived in a Honda City car; one pointed a revolver at him, his cell phone, car keys and cash were taken, his face was covered, his mouth was taped and his hands were tied, and he was forced into the dicky of the Honda City car. For about two days he was held captive and moved between places. He was chained, blindfolded and given drugs, and he heard his captors address each other by nicknames. The captors repeatedly phoned his father demanding ransom, first Rs. 5 crores and later Rs. 1 crore, threatening that the victim and family would be killed if it was not paid. The father raised money from several lenders, some of whom had marked packets of notes with initials. Money was thrown from a moving train as instructed, and the victim was released. Police registered an FIR, arrested the accused and, on their disclosure statements, recovered cash, firearms, the Honda City car, and the victim's driving licence and tape from the car's dicky. Telephone call records were collected, but no certificate was obtained for them. No identification parade was held. The victim identified the accused in later testimony.

value: The victim, a married woman, was sleeping in the matrimonial house in the early hours of 20 September 1999 when the accused persons came to her room. According to the victim's statement, the husband and his younger brother had earlier beaten her. Two other family members held her arms, the husband sprinkled kerosene on her and the brother lit a matchstick, setting her ablaze. Neighbours extinguished the fire. The accused persons took the victim to a hospital, where she was found to have about 100% burns. The attending doctor certified that she was fit to make a statement. A judicial magistrate then recorded her statement in the presence of the medical officer, and the doctor again certified that she remained fit during the recording. The victim died within a few hours. A post-mortem found the burns to be ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. Following a disclosure by the husband, police recovered an empty plastic kerosene container. The victim's father and brother, examined as witnesses, did not support the prosecution account. The brother said the husband had been with him at his house on the night of the incident and that they learned of the burns at about 4 a.m. Hospital records showed that the husband had brought the victim to hospital and had her admitted. The victim's statement also alleged years of dowry demands and repeated beatings by the in-laws.

He stated that the accused then tied a rope around the victim's neck and suspended the body from the shed roof, and threatened him with death if he disclosed the incident. He said the events lasted about an hour and that he raised no alarm. He disclosed the incident to three other persons about three days later. The investigating officer's spot map recorded no source of light in the locality. The post-mortem examination found death was due to asphyxia from constriction of the neck and not hanging by rope. The friend was held down and beaten with iron rods, while the victim was taken to the rear of the bus and raped repeatedly by several men in turn, including anal and oral sex. A bite-mark comparison linked two accused to bite marks on the victim. Articles belonging to the victim and friend were recovered on the accused's disclosure statements. The victim gave several statements in hospital, including a later one written in gestures and writing, naming the accused.

value: A land dispute between closely related families had strained relations after the victim cultivated land that had been leased to a relative. On the evening of 15 September 1994, the victim's wife, while cutting grass in her field, saw the three accused working in a nearby field and heard them say they would not spare the victim because he had beaten a relative. The accused left the field carrying an iron rod and twigs, and the wife followed them to a place where a relative was sitting injured on the road and the victim was standing nearby. The prosecution case was that one accused struck the victim on the head with an iron rod and stabbed him on the cheek, while the others beat his legs and hands with twigs. The accused then threw their weapons away and left. The victim was taken to a government hospital by the wife and another person and was declared dead. A post-mortem recorded six serious bleeding injuries to the scalp. Police registered a complaint from the wife and, separately, a case based on the injured relative's statement. Bloodstained iron rod, twigs and earth were seized. The accused were arrested on 17 September 1994 from a bus-stand, when blood-stained clothing worn by one accused was seized. All material objects were sent for chemical analysis.

value: In December 1980, a large number of people who had bought country liquor from a single licensed liquor vend in a village and consumed it fell seriously ill. Thirty-six of them died and forty-four lost their eyesight permanently. Post-mortem examinations of the deceased found methyl alcohol in their viscera. Doctors who examined the surviving victims attributed their loss of vision to intake of methyl alcohol. Statements made by the victims immediately after they fell ill, and by close relatives of the deceased, consistently identified the vend as the source of the liquor. Police produced and sealed bottles of the liquor from victims, and after the accused were interrogated they recovered empty bottles and corks used for preparing and storing the liquor. The vend's records were seized and were found to have been forged. The prosecution case was that the accused, as contractors of the licensed vend, adulterated liquor with methyl alcohol and sold it through their agents, knowing its toxic effect. After the tragedy received media coverage, the accused's staff were said to have thrown remaining bottles into a river and canal. Some bottles recovered from the canal were not tested for methyl alcohol, and the investigation was criticised for lapses.

value: The victim, a woman whose husband had died about eleven years earlier, lived in a joint family house with her son, her daughter and the accused, her brother-in-law. On the evening of 23 August 2007, the accused came to the house in a drunken state, abused the victim and her children and threatened to kill them. An elderly woman in the house took the son into an adjoining room and bolted it from outside, and sent the daughter to the house of the victim's maternal uncle. From the room's window, the son heard the victim crying out and saw the accused taking her towards the house of another person. Hours later, the accused opened the door and told the son that the victim had run away, and told him to tell the maternal uncle the same. Under threat from the accused and another person, the son told the uncle so. The uncle came to the house in the early hours of 24 August, and the son and uncle reported the victim missing at the police station. On 25 August the uncle received a call that the victim's body was hanging from a tree in a forest. The body was found hanging from a pine branch, a plastic rope tied around the neck. value: On the evening of 19 June 1995, an altercation reportedly took place between the victim and one of the accused over a sum of money, near a grocery shop in the village; the victim was said to have slapped that accused during the scuffle. Later that evening, a group of about sixteen persons, armed with sticks, a sword, an axe and an iron pipe, allegedly entered the victim's house, dragged him out, and assaulted his hands and legs. The assault allegedly continued while he was dragged along the road and to a field, where his right palm was reportedly cut off. The victim's wife, who witnessed part of the incident, reportedly hid in a cattle shed for about two hours before informing a neighbour, and a complaint was lodged the following day. The victim's body was found in a field on 21 June 1995 without the right palm, which was found at some distance. Eyewitnesses, including the victim's wife, father and two neighbours, gave consistent accounts that the rifle-armed accused was present. The father said he gave dowry beyond his means, gave a gold chain about a year after the marriage, and paid cash sums on later occasions, but the in-laws continued to demand money and beat the victim. The victim had written letters about the harassment. In February 1994 the victim's father was informed that the victim had died in hospital, and he alleged that the in-laws had administered poison. A first information report was lodged the next day against four family members, who were arrested. The prosecution relied on the oral statements of the victim's father and brother and on several letters written by the victim, including one to her father about the in-laws and the gold chain, one to a brother-in-law saying her husband beat her daily, and one about her mother-in-law's dislike of her cooking. A written memorandum dated January 1992, said to record a settlement executed by the in-laws before panchayat members, was also relied upon, though no panchayat member was examined. The death was attributed to organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.

value: The prosecution case is that the victim had a dispute with one of the accused over the cultivation of a plot of land, which led to an exchange of abuses and threats that the victim would be killed. The uncle heard a noise and returned to find six accused standing outside the house, armed with a lathi, two guns, two axes and a pitchfork. One accused allegedly directed that the victim be killed. Two accused fired three shots each from the entrance of the house, two others struck the victim with axes, and another struck with a pitchfork. The victim died on the spot. Other villagers arrived, and the accused threatened them before running away. The uncle dictated a written complaint immediately afterwards. It was scribed by a teacher who reached the spot around 12:45 pm, and was taken to the police station and registered as a first information report. The post-mortem doctor recorded six firearm entry wounds, several incised wounds and firearm exit wounds, and opined that death occurred between 12 and 12:30 pm. The investigation included a site plan and the seizure of guns. The ballistic report was not proved. Two eyewitnesses gave evidence supporting the prosecution account.

value: The victim, a woman married to the accused in June 1994, died in October 1995 from severe burn injuries, about seventeen months after the marriage. The accused, a police constable, lived with her at his posting. Over the marriage the accused was said to drink alcohol heavily, often arriving at the victim's parents' house drunk, and repeatedly demanded money from the victim and her parents, at one stage insisting she bring several thousand rupees from her family. He also beat and ill-treated the victim, including while intoxicated. The victim's father and mother, a brother-in-law and a relative each described these incidents in evidence, saying the victim had complained to them and that her parents had sent money on two occasions. The victim also wrote a letter to her father describing ill-treatment. When the victim's mother and a sister-in-law visited the accused's house, the accused allegedly abused them and beat them with shoes. On the day of the incident, around 8 a.m., only the victim and the accused were in the house. Evidence showed that the victim had been doused with kerosene and set alight in the kitchen, and a bottle of kerosene lay in the room. Broken bangles were found in the room. The post-mortem and forensic reports showed kerosene on the body and burns heavier on the upper body, including a burnt blouse. The accused's explanation was that the victim's nylon sari caught fire accidentally while she was boiling water on the oven. At the hospital the victim told her father that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire, and she died that evening. The father lodged a complaint the same day. The investigating officer recorded statements, arranged the post-mortem, obtained the forensic report and filed a charge-sheet.

value: Five women living in one house were found dead on 17 December 2012, with some bodies in a courtyard and others in a room. A relative who was alerted by a child living in the house went to the scene and saw blood from the nose and mouth of the victims and marks of injury on their necks. A post-mortem examination found that all five died of asphyxia due to strangulation, and the deaths were homicidal. The investigating officer prepared a site map and seized a glass whisky bottle, a torch, six strands of black hair from one victim's hand, two white buttons, blood-stained soil and a woollen shawl. Fingerprints lifted from the bottle were reported to match one accused. A forensic report found a shirt button and the buttons from the scene to be similar, and a hair report identified only human hair. Following statements made by the accused, a motorcycle, a sum of cash and a silver anklet were recovered, and one accused's shirt was seized. The prosecution alleged that the killings were committed during a robbery. A child witness said that the accused had come to the house the previous night and that, in the early morning, she had found the door locked from outside. She identified the accused as the persons she had seen with the victims. A witness heard of the accused's visit only through a telephone call, and a motorcycle witness gave conflicting descriptions. The gold ornaments and pearl necklace on the victims' bodies were recorded in the site plan.

value: The victim organisation, a food corporation, alleged that a depot in-charge and other staff conspired with a transporter and a contractor to misappropriate urea fertiliser bags during March 1980. A complaint dated December 1981 led to registration of a first information report, which initially referred to 540 bags. Wagons carrying fertiliser were placed at a railway station for unloading, and delivery was signed for in the delivery book on 24 and 25 March 1980. The prosecution alleged that 500 bags were handed over to a representative who signed gate passes for two trucks, each said to carry 250 bags to the depot. The accused responsible for receipt at the depot gate register and the in-charge who maintained the godown registers were said to have entered the arrival of these bags, although the bags were never delivered. The investigation concluded that the entire 1040 bags were misappropriated. Evidence included depositions of the two truck owners, the drivers and a cleaner, who stated that one truck was diverted to a different location and the other was never used for carrying fertiliser. The gate register, arrival tally book, daily receipt register and godown stock register were examined, together with a chart prepared in October 1982 showing delivery of the 500 bags. A government document examiner, an audit assistant manager, a physical verification officer and the investigating officer also testified. Defence evidence came from a retired assistant depot manager.

value: On the night of 10 July 1988, the victim, an army officer, and a colleague visited a hotel on the main road in Ahmednagar. The prosecution alleged that a quarrel broke out at the hotel between the accused and the two visitors, and that chilli powder was thrown into the eyes of the visitors, after which they ran out. The victim was allegedly chased by the accused and assaulted with a gupti, a knife-type weapon, and fell on the road. A beat constable on patrol nearby stated that he saw the accused chase and assault the victim, and that the accused was wearing a black sando banian and a lungi. The constable took the victim by rickshaw to the police station and then to the civil hospital. At the hospital, a Special Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration from the victim around midnight, in which the victim described the assailant's clothing. An offence was registered on that basis. The accused was arrested in the early hours of the following day, and blood-stained clothing, a vest and a lungi, was seized from him, along with a gupti recovered on his information. Chemical analysis found the blood group on the clothing matched the victim's blood group. The victim died on 23 July 1988 and the investigation was extended to a homicide offence. The prosecution examined 14 witnesses. Two independent witnesses and the panch witnesses to the seizure did not support the prosecution. The medical evidence was said to be consistent with the eyewitness account.

value: On a day in March 1998 at about 5.30 pm, the victim was riding a motorcycle with two companions when a group of four men stopped it near a lane. One of the men asked the victim to get down to talk. When the victim got down, one attacker struck the victim on the back with a lathi. The victim ran toward a lane to escape. Two other men allegedly caught hold of the victim's arms, and the accused who had the pistol fired at close range at the victim's face, killing the victim instantly. Three eyewitnesses, two of them the victim's companions on the motorcycle and one nearby, described these acts consistently. The defence alleged no eyewitness was present. The post-mortem found a gunshot wound to the left eye and brain, with gunpowder in the eyes, and nine other injuries on the back, arms, chest and head. The doctor opined that the shot was fired from about one foot away. Following a disclosure, a country-made pistol was recovered from a house. Forensic examination found the pistol operative, but the barrel marks on the bullet were insufficient for decisive matching. The FIR was registered at a police station on the same day at 6 pm, and an inquest was conducted at the scene.

value: On 16 October 2016, around midday, the victim was with several friends near a medical store when a pillion rider on a motorcycle attacked him with a sharp-edged machete, striking the right side of his neck, and then fled. The victim was declared dead on arrival at hospital. According to the prosecution, the victim was dressed in uniform during a march organised by an association that day, and his throat was cut in a single blow. The case was first registered as a murder by local police, and four persons were arrested within weeks. A fifth person, the accused, was arrested later. The investigation was then taken over by a national investigating agency, which alleged that the accused and four co-accused conspired to kill members of that association. The prosecution relied on call data records showing frequent telephone contact between the accused and co-accused before and after the incident, bank account details, and a seized banner bearing the photographs of all the accused. It also relied on a disclosure leading to a letter listing earlier killings, and on an allegation that the accused had organised indoctrination classes about eight to nine months earlier that the co-accused attended. One co-accused was alleged to have named the accused as the mastermind. The accused denied any personal animosity toward the victim and said nothing incriminating had been recovered from him.

The victim left home in the morning, saying he would visit a relative in a nearby village and then report for duty. He did not return by evening, and his mobile phone was switched off. The next morning the victim's daughter was told by a forest guard that he had not reported for duty. She then telephoned a person who lived opposite her house and asked for a contact number at the village. At about 7:15 am on the following day, the police received a telephone call from one of the accused reporting that the victim had died of a gunshot. A police team went towards the place of occurrence. Later that day the victim's daughter gave a statement naming two accused as the shooters, saying she had learned this from police when they came to the village. The police took the two accused, two local witnesses and the daughter to a forest about two kilometres from the house. There the victim's body was found, along with a bag and two pellet marks on nearby bushes. Both accused were said to have made disclosure statements in the presence of the two witnesses, leading to the body and a single-barrel gun with cartridges being recovered; the gun was licensed to a third person and was found at his house. Forensic examination reported that a cartridge had been fired from the gun and that gunshot residue on the victim's clothes indicated distant firing. The post-mortem found multiple perforated gunshot wounds and recorded death from cardio-respiratory failure and hypovolemic shock due to gunshot injury. Both witnesses to the disclosure statements later denied in cross-examination that any such statement was made in their presence. The investigating officer's accounts of when the death became known were said to be contradictory, and no call records were produced to verify the telephone call. The alleged motive was a land dispute with one of the accused.

value: On 22 October 1992 at about 11 a.m., a quarrel broke out between the accused and the victim over the victim's cultivation of land that the accused had been given for cultivation. The two had a pre-existing land dispute, and the victim was related to a co-accused, who was also related to the accused. The accused stopped the victim on his way to the field and told him not to cultivate the land. The argument grew heated with raised voices, and about 50 to 60 villagers gathered. A co-accused, cycling past, stopped and intervened. The victim told him not to interfere and to go home. The co-accused took a country-made pistol from his trouser pocket, pointed it at the victim, and fired. The victim was struck by splinters on the forehead near his eye, on his lips and on his shoulder, and bled. The victim testified that the accused urged the co-accused to kill him; an eyewitness testified that the accused told the co-accused to beat the victim. A medical officer said the injuries were caused by firearm splinters. After the firing the co-accused fled and the accused followed him. The victim lodged a report at a police chowki, a case was registered, and the investigating officer examined the victim and eyewitnesses and seized blood-stained clothing. Several witnesses did not support the prosecution.

value: On 10 July 1999, the victim, an advocate, was sitting in his residential office dictating to his stenographer, with his clerk present. At about 5:30 pm, the accused, a police constable, entered the office in an inebriated condition, claiming to be a beat officer, and asked for water. After drinking the water, the accused pulled out his service pistol, pointed it at the victim and said he would kill ten people that day. The accused asked the victim to stand with raised hands and directed the clerk and stenographer to leave the room. The accused then moved around the table towards the victim and pulled the lever to ready the weapon. The victim lunged and pushed the accused's hand upward, and a bullet struck the ceiling. No one was injured. The accused tried to fire again, but a bullet fell from the pistol. Household members entered and raised an alarm, and the accused fled, leaving a wireless set behind. Police arrived within about 10 to 15 minutes and arrested the accused nearby with the pistol still in hand. A medical examination recorded that the accused was under the influence of alcohol; the accused declined to give urine or blood samples. A forensic report found that the cartridge recovered from the office was fired from the accused's pistol. The stenographer testified that he saw the shot fired through a mesh door, and the clerk testified to the accused's drunken state and to hearing the shot. The victim testified to the sequence of events.

value: On a night in February, the complainant's family had returned home from a wedding function in a nearby village with food. Police recovered sticks, a blood-stained stone, glass splinters, pieces of wood, broken door pieces, a broken bulb and blood-stained soil from the house, and an axe from one accused. Blood marks were also found on a path outside the house. The post-mortem found one fatal sharp-edged head injury, which the doctor said could have been caused by the recovered axe. The injured man had incised wounds on the face and back of the skull and a facial bone fracture, which the doctor said could be caused by an axe. value: On the intervening night of 2 and 3 August 2006, at about 2.30 to 3.00 am, a fire broke out in a small house of three rooms. The house was occupied by the accused, the accused's husband, the husband's first wife, the first wife's two children, the husband's parents and a servant who occupied one room. The husband had gone to another town that day to buy tractor tyres, and the mother-in-law had gone to her daughter's home. The accused came out of the house without any injury. The first wife and her daughter ran out with burn injuries, while the son died inside the house. The father-in-law, who had been sleeping on a cot outside, woke in the confusion and arranged for a jeep to take the injured to hospital. The first wife and daughter died the next day from their burns. Police seized the daughter's burnt frock from the scene under a panchnama and sent it for chemical analysis, which reported kerosene residues. A kerosene can said to smell of kerosene was recovered from nearby bushes at the accused's instance, but it was not sent for chemical analysis. The father-in-law stated that the accused had made an extra-judicial confession to him that kerosene had been sprinkled and the fire set. A sister of the first wife gave evidence of an oral dying declaration, and a police head constable recorded a separate dying declaration. The first wife's declaration said the household slept in the house with a lantern lit at night, and that cooking and tractor diesel were kept there. Medical evidence was presented on the cause of the deaths.

value: On the day before the incident, the accused quarrelled with the victim, who was the accused's uncle, and abused him; the victim sharply reprimanded the accused. The next morning, at about 10:30 to 11:00 a.m., the victim was walking towards the village bus stand when the accused approached from the opposite direction carrying a wooden side of a cot frame. The accused abused the victim for shouting at and insulting him the previous day, said he would teach him a lesson, and struck the victim once on the head. The victim fell down, and the accused ran away with the wooden piece. Two of the victim's sons, who were standing outside a nearby shop, took their bleeding father to Civil Hospital, Giddarbaha, from where he was referred to Dayanand Medical College, Ludhiana. The victim died the following day. The complainant son gave a written statement to a police officer, which was endorsed and sent for registration of an FIR. Police visited the spot, prepared a rough site plan and lifted blood-stained earth. At the hospital, an inquest was prepared, and a post-mortem found eight injuries, the main one on the head; the doctor opined the cause of death was shock and haemorrhage from the head injury. The accused was arrested some weeks later and, in police presence, indicated where the blood-stained wooden piece was concealed in a wheat chaff room at the accused's residence; it was recovered. Chemical examination found the blood on the piece and on the spot earth matched the victim. Two eyewitnesses, the victim's sons, testified that the accused struck the victim's head with the wooden piece.

value: On the night of 24 June 1987, the victim was travelling on a scooter with two companions on a separate scooter toward a village to attend a marriage. Near a road turn at about 9.30 pm, the two companions say that in the scooter light they saw three uniformed men on the road, one carrying a stick and two carrying rifles. The victim was hit, collapsed, and was taken to a hospital in the presence of police, but died on the way. The two companions escaped to the village. The FIR was lodged by one companion, and a separate case was registered on a rival version describing an armed criminal group and police retaliatory fire, in which two empty cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. Villagers and police arrived at the scene. Three uniformed constables were on patrol that night and had left the police station with rifles and 50 rounds each. Ballistic examination found that some empty cartridges at the spot were fired from the service rifles of two of the constables, while two others were not matched to any of the three. The autopsy showed the fatal injury came from a .12 bore gun, which was not recovered from any of the accused. One witness claimed to have seen the accused fire a country-made pistol, and the accused were said to have remained at the spot after the incident.

value: The victim, a police constable working as record keeper at a police station, was using the station's official telephone in the reporting room for five to seven minutes. The duty officer, a sub-inspector, told the victim to free the line because urgent calls might come in, but the victim continued the call. Around 5.55 pm the duty officer asked the accused, a guard posted at the station and carrying a semi-automatic fire carbine, to ask the victim to end the call. The accused entered the room, placed a hand on the victim's shoulder and asked the victim to end the call. The prosecution's initial account was that the victim playfully pushed the accused while holding the carbine. During the struggle the carbine became entangled in the chain attached to the accused's belt, and five rounds fired. Five bullets struck the victim in the neck and chest. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. An offence was first registered on the duty officer's statement. The victim's father complained to senior police officers, and the investigation was transferred to the Crime Branch, which alleged that the victim had seen the accused and the duty officer in a compromising position and that they had threatened to kill him. Ballistic reports recorded close-range firing. A later report stated that the carbine could be cocked by entanglement with a chain if the change lever was not at the safety position, and would then fire if the trigger was pressed. Eyewitness accounts described the entanglement and accidental firing. A witness said he heard the accused tell the duty officer that the accused's children would be ruined, and heard the duty officer's reply. Several other persons present did not support the prosecution.

value: In the late evening of the incident, the victim was allegedly assaulted with lathis in an open street in front of a house in a village, by several men identified as the accused. Two eyewitnesses said they saw the assault. A named first information report was lodged the next morning at about 10 am by a village chowkidar of a neighbouring village, who said no eyewitness had informed her; she had come to the spot after hearing loud noises and found the body near a temple. The autopsy recorded lacerations to the left temple and left ear, contusions on the left thigh, rib fractures on both sides, lung contusions, and extradural haemorrhage in the left temporal region. The statement attributed the burning to the accused and two in-laws, who had held the victim while kerosene was poured. An FIR was registered on that statement. value: On the morning of 17 April 1988, the victim was being taken by his son to a hospital for treatment, with a companion riding pillion. Upon reaching a particular house, eleven persons attacked them with country-made bombs, lathis and tabbal (shovels). The victim received multiple injuries and died during treatment. The companion ran off and hid in a nearby house for about two hours, suffering numerous injuries, including lacerated wounds and serious damage to his left eye. The victim's son was found alive near a tree close to the scene. He was taken to a government hospital and then to a private hospital, where he died the same day. Post-mortem examinations were performed on both bodies by two doctors. A medical officer who examined the companion opined that his lacerated wounds could have been caused by country-made bombs. The police reached the scene at about 11.15 a.m. after a report recorded at 11.00 a.m. at the companion's instance. The FIR recorded the incident time as 8.15 a.m. Three eyewitnesses, including the companion, the victim's wife and a relative of the victim, testified that the accused were present at the scene and attacked the victim with bombs, lathis and shovels. The investigating sub-inspector found the complicity of all eleven persons and filed a challan.

value: The victim, who had been living with his in-laws for about three to four months, was found dead inside the house of the accused by the victim's brother, who had gone there after learning that the victim had been assaulted. On the morning of 14 May 2004, at about 6:00 a.m., the accused attacked the victim with an iron locking plate inside a store where the victim was working. The store belonged to the brother of the accused's grandfather. The prosecution alleged there was no motive, no provocation and no premeditation. An eyewitness saw the incident. After the assault, the accused took the object out of the store, walked to a nearby bus stand, returned and left the object in the shop, then went back to the bus stand and sat on a chair without attempting to leave. Before the incident, the accused had been an in-patient at a government hospital in Bhiwani, Haryana, from 17 to 26 November 2003. The records noted anxiety neurosis with reactive depression, symptoms of acid peptic disease and mild hypertension. The treatment given was akin to that for schizophrenia, and the medicine Thioril was prescribed. After the incident, a government doctor examined the accused. She later certified that the accused had chronic schizophrenia, probably from around age 14 or 15, and was not fit to stand trial. A later certificate, issued after in-patient treatment, stated the accused could stand trial. Her statement was recorded about sixteen years after the occurrence. An uncle of the accused testified about the earlier treatment. A relative of the accused's grandfather who was examined found no abnormality. The doctor who physically examined the accused after the incident stated the accused was mentally well.

The second accused was arrested at about 4 am and produced a bag with gold ornaments; blood-stained clothing was seized from both. The father identified the ornaments at an identification parade conducted with independent witnesses. value: Late on the night of the incident, the victim was talking with a friend near a car consultancy shop in a slum area when one of the accused passing by approached him, and a verbal exchange followed. Shortly afterwards, the accused arrived with others and a fight broke out. The victim's friend was struck on the head with a sickle and a sword and was bleeding. The victim was then severely attacked with a sickle and a sword, receiving multiple wounds to the hands, wrist, arm, shoulder and chest. A neighbour came out of his house during the assault and asked what the fighting was about. The injured friend asked a rickshaw driver known to them to watch the victim and then went with a neighbour to the police station to report the incident. Police took the victim to hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem examination found multiple injuries, including a stab wound to the right chest that cut the ribs and entered the lung. The doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death, and that the injuries were caused by sharp-edged weapons. Three eyewitnesses gave oral evidence, including the injured friend, the neighbour and the rickshaw driver. The rickshaw driver stated that the injured friend told him what had happened. Following statements made by the accused in police custody, weapons were recovered in the presence of panch witnesses. A chargesheet was filed after investigation.

value: The accused married the victim in October 1992, and a male child was born to them in December 1993. Earlier, the victim had lodged a first information report alleging cruelty by the accused and had filed a complaint under Sections 107/151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and a petition seeking maintenance for herself and her child. value: On an evening at about 9.45 pm, the victim was sitting in the courtyard of the home with the victim's wife, talking. Four men from the same village came to the courtyard. The prosecution alleged that they said they would teach the victim a lesson for refusing to give them jaggery (gur), and that one of them fired a firearm at the victim. The shot struck the victim's right chest and arm. The victim's son and grandson, who were nearby, heard the shot, reached the courtyard within moments and reported seeing the four men fleeing. The victim was taken to a government hospital, where a doctor declared the victim dead. A written report was lodged the following day and a case was registered. The investigating officer inspected the scene, prepared an inquest report and a site plan, and seized a torch, a lantern, bloodstained soil, a bloodstained cot and bedding. Acting on information given by one accused, police recovered a 12-bore country-made pistol and one empty cartridge from a field near a transformer. The post-mortem found two firearm wounds of entry, on the right arm and right chest, with blackening and tattooing around them; death was due to shock and haemorrhage from firearm injuries, and both wounds could have been caused by one bullet. Eyewitnesses testified that the accused were armed and that one of them fired on the exhortation of the others. One eyewitness explained the source of light at the scene. The investigating officer's account differed on whether the shooting was instigated by others. Several discrepancies in the prosecution evidence were noted.

value: The body of the victim was found in a paddy field in the early morning of 17 August 1989 by a passer-by on his way to work. A postmortem examination found six antemortem injuries on the left side of the head, fractured into multiple fragments, plus abraded contusions on the right wrist and left knee. The head injuries were sufficient to cause death and could have been caused by a coconut scraper. The medical expert estimated death about 30 to 35 hours before the postmortem. The prosecution alleged that the accused and a co-accused were in an illicit relationship, and that the victim often stayed at the co-accused's house. The victim's mother and sister said the victim left for that house around 7:30 PM on 16 August. The co-accused's two children said the victim left their house around 9:00 PM and did not return. A witness said he saw the back of a person he assumed was the accused entering the house around 11:30 PM. The prosecution alleged that during an altercation about the relationship, the accused struck the victim on the head repeatedly with a coconut scraper, dragged the body out, and carried it about one kilometre to the paddy field. A taxi driver said he saw a man he identified as the accused at a bus stand at about 5:30 AM on 17 August, wearing a shirt, lungi and towel. A bag said to contain blood-stained clothes, a blanket and a head towel belonging to the accused was said to have been recovered on 27 August. value: On the evening of 10 April 2004 the victim left a workplace on his motorcycle after receiving two phone calls, saying he had to go to a market. The next morning his family reported him missing. His body was later found lying in a field with his throat tied with cloth, one eye badly injured and injuries to the head. The post-mortem doctor found an incised wound that, in the doctor's view, was caused by a sharp-edged weapon. Investigators recorded statements from several persons. One witness said he saw four young men on a motorcycle carrying sticks near a bypass that evening, one of them with blood-stained clothing, and noted a registration number. Another said he saw three young men on a motorcycle holding sticks at a road junction around 10 pm and recognised one of them. A third said he saw the victim seated on a motorcycle with one of the accused at a junction. After a surrender, the accused were said to have made an extra-judicial confession before a village sarpanch, who also said he had seen the victim earlier that evening. Police recovered sticks, a pair of trousers and a mobile phone. Forensic tests reported blood of the same group as the victim on the sticks and trousers. No sharp-edged weapon was recovered. The recoveries were not made in the presence of any independent witness. The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitness to the killing.

value: The victim was travelling to a nearby town in an auto-rickshaw on a morning in November 2001, with two co-passengers. One accused gave a confessional statement, after which an axe, a sword and a knife were recovered from bushes in a field. Several eyewitnesses described the sequence of the assault, the weapons used and the role of each accused. Among them, several said one accused struck the victim's head with a stone. The prosecution alleged that the co-accused told the accused that one son was causing trouble and should be killed. The accused then fired a country-made pistol. The bullet struck the victim's left breast, and she died immediately. The targeted son said he bent below the cot. The witnesses gave differing accounts of where people were sitting and whether the son had stood up. The son lodged a written report at a police station at midnight on the same day, stating that the two men ran away towards the north. The police seized a cartridge tikli from the wound, a 12 bore cartridge from the cot, and 12 pellets from the wound. The post-mortem recovered 55 pellets from the body. The pistol was never recovered. The pellets and tikli were not sent for ballistic examination. Blood-stained clothes and soil samples were sent to a chemical examiner, but no report was received. Another son who was present and the scribe of the report were not examined. A village head said he heard the firing and learned of the death later from a passer-by, who was also not examined. value: On the evening of the incident, the victim and the accused were walking a few steps ahead of the victim's sister-in-law, who was returning from a local market. She saw them grapple with each other and then saw the accused stab the victim several times with a knife the accused was carrying. The victim collapsed and the accused ran away. The victim was first taken to a nearby private clinic and then advised to go to a hospital, where the victim was declared dead on arrival. A post-mortem the next day recorded multiple incised stab wounds on the body. One wound entered the left chest cavity, injuring the pericardium and the tip of the left ventricle; the examining doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, which was due to shock and haemorrhage. The doctor stated that the injuries were possible with the recovered knife, which had been produced in a sealed parcel. An FIR was registered the same day based on the eyewitness's statement. Shortly afterwards, police received information and found the accused coming from the side of a drain, carrying a blood-stained knife and wearing a blood-stained shirt. The accused was apprehended and the knife and shirt were recovered. Forensic analysis found that the victim's blood matched blood on the knife. The eyewitness described the sequence of events in detail, having watched from a short distance, and was cross-examined at length without any material discrediting her testimony.

value: The victim's father owned agricultural land and a house in a village. In the morning of a September day in 2001, the victim went with four farm workers to build a check dam on the family land. The father packed their lunch at midday and visited the field. Work stopped at about 3.30 pm, and the group set off for the village. Near a particular landholding at about 4 pm, several accused allegedly appeared and said that the victim's side had killed a member of their family and that they would take revenge in the same manner. The accused were said to be armed with a jambiya, axes and sickles, and the victim was beaten and fell. The father alleged that he was threatened and hid in bushes until after sunset. He then returned home and told family members. A written complaint was lodged at the police station early the next morning, and an FIR was registered. Investigation led to a charge sheet against the accused and others. Twenty-seven witnesses were examined. Four workers and the father were presented as eyewitnesses, along with another witness. The medical jurist described decomposition of the body and an estimated time of death more than 24 hours before autopsy. Witnesses said it had rained heavily for about three days before the incident. The investigating officer described recoveries of axes, a koyta, a jambiya and sickles made on the basis of statements of the accused. The complainant said police showed him the weapons on the day of the incident. No serological opinion on the weapons was obtained.

value: The victim was a long-serving cash collector and clerk employed by the accused, who ran a wood business. On 15 July 1993 the victim and a companion were collecting business proceeds from shops. While the victim was inside a shop, two men snatched a bag holding the collection from the companion at gunpoint and fled on a motorcycle. The accused reported this as a robbery to the police. The initial investigation found the report to be false, but the case was later reassigned to another officer. On 17 July 1993 the accused had the victim brought from his home through an employee to the police station for inquiry. According to the later investigation report, the victim was then held at the police station until 23 July 1993 and was tortured during interrogation about the robbery. Late on 23 July he was taken to a hospital by police personnel and was admitted under an unknown name. He died in the early hours of 24 July 1993. A complaint by the accused alleged that police personnel had beaten the victim to death. The post mortem report recorded ante mortem cut incisions on both buttocks. The cause of death could not be ascertained and poisoning was ruled out. Section 161 statements of the victim's widow, son and brother were recorded. Under the investigation report, no police station entry of the custody was made.

value: On a day in early April, the victim, a minor boy, went out in his car to play badminton and did not return home that evening. Later that night, his family began receiving telephone calls from unknown callers claiming the boy was in their custody and demanding a ransom of one crore rupees, with threats to kill the boy and harm the family if the police were informed. The family gathered cash from various sources and, on instructions from the callers, left the money in a car at a hospital area and then went to another location. Shortly afterwards the boy was found standing in a market area and was brought home. According to the victim, three men had stopped his car on the way home from the playground, one holding a pistol. He was robbed of his watch, ATM card, identity card, gold chain and cash, blindfolded, and kept confined overnight in a room, where he heard the men calling each other by name. The family did not report the matter to police for about two weeks. Police acted on source information about a kidnapping gang and registered a case without a complaint from the family. The investigating officer traced two mobile numbers used for the ransom calls through the service provider and SIM sale records. Several men were arrested and disclosure statements were recorded, followed by alleged recoveries of cash, a motorcycle, watches, mobile phones, a car and an air pistol. The victim later identified the accused at a later stage of the proceedings, and call detail records were produced.

value: The victim, who had been arraigned as an accused in a criminal case registered at a police station, came to that police station late at night, accompanied by his advocate and two sisters, to surrender. The prosecution case is that two police officers, the accused, assaulted the victim with fists and sticks at separate intervals inside the police station, causing multiple injuries across his body, after which he became unconscious and was placed in a lockup. He was taken to a civil hospital and declared dead early the following morning. Two sisters testified that they saw the beatings, and a third detainee in the lockup also gave evidence. The sisters described blows landing on the back, arms, chest, thighs and ankles. A telegram sent by one sister to the state police headquarters alleged custodial torture, and a formal complaint followed about three weeks after the incident. The post-mortem examination recorded multiple external abrasions and bruises and internal injuries, including fractures of the sternum and ribs and ruptures of the lung, liver and spleen. The medical jurist opined that the injuries were fresh, occurring within six to eight hours of death, and that a person with such injuries could not climb stairs without support. An inquest witness described red dust on the clothing, and the jail soil was said to be red. The advocate was not examined as a witness.

value: On the afternoon of 8 September 1992, the victim went to a riverside ghat to bathe, accompanied by his son and his brother. Near the ghat, a group of men approached from the direction of a park. According to the eyewitness accounts, the group included the accused, who was carrying a country-made pistol, and other persons armed with a danda, kanta and knives. The group confronted the victim, caught hold of him and assaulted him with kanta and knives. On hearing his cries for help, the victim's son, another witness and the victim's brother ran towards the spot. As they approached, the accused fired a shot into the air from the pistol, after which the group fled from the scene through the south-western side. The victim was found dead on the steps of the ghat with his body partly in the water. A post-mortem examination recorded multiple incised and stab wounds on the head, face, neck, chest, back and arm, and the doctor opined that death was possibly caused by shock and haemorrhage from sharp-edged weapons. A written report was lodged at the police station shortly after the incident, and the investigating officers recorded statements of witnesses. Prior litigation between the families over property formed the background to the incident. No country-made pistol or cartridge was recovered from the scene.

value: On the night of 13 November 2011, at about 9.30 p.m., the victim and his mother were sleeping at their house in a village in Dewas district. Someone called the victim's name from outside and the victim opened the door. The victim's mother testified that she heard a gunshot and ran towards him. A second shot then struck the victim in the chest and he fell. Going outside, the mother saw the victim's wife and son standing on the opposite side of the house. She also saw two individuals with covered faces fleeing on a motorcycle. A country-made pistol was later recovered from the accused. A ballistic report found that the bullet recovered from the victim's body had been fired from that pistol. The prosecution case was that the location of the pistol was disclosed by a co-accused, who has since died, and that this disclosure led to the recovery of the pistol and to the arrest of the accused. No eyewitness identified the accused as a participant in the shooting. The case against the accused rested on the recovery of the pistol and the ballistic report. A First Information Report was registered on 13 November 2011, and a chargesheet was filed against several persons.
